llm: Claude Sonnet (one fresh agent, prompt = evidence sheet only, srlab.rag.prompt)
prompt:
You are helping a search-ranking engineer understand one failed search. Use ONLY the evidence sheet below. Every number you write must appear in the sheet exactly as written there. Cite retrieved cases as [1], [2], [3].

EVIDENCE SHEET

This search: member 304 asked "a fantasy movie that isn't animated". The ranker put Aladdin (1992) first; the better match was Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002).
Why Aladdin (1992) (TemGX links, CATGX structure): 1 of 3 from other people's ratings, 2 of 3 from the title's recent raters; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Example links: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002) – user 297, rating 3.0 on 2015-12-08; Aladdin (1992) – user 425, rating 4.5 on 2015-12-27; Aladdin (1992) – user 533, rating 4.5 on 2016-04-04.
Why Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002): 1 of 3 from the title's recent raters, 2 of 3 from the member's own ratings; structure: a taste path from the member to the title.
Check by deletion: the graph model prefers Aladdin (1992) with 73% confidence; deleting Aladdin (1992)'s explanation links gives 46%; deleting Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002)'s gives 81%; deleting random links from the same period gives 72%.

Retrieved from 343 verified past diagnoses (most similar mechanism first):
  [1] member 246, "a comedy for grown-ups, not a kids movie": Hunt for Red October, The (1990) ranked above Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan (2006). Why: 1 of 3 from other people's ratings, 1 of 3 from the title's recent raters, 1 of 3 from the member's own ratings; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Fixes that worked when re-ranked: understand “not” in the request.
  [2] member 142, "a musical, but not a romance": Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, The (2005) ranked above Robin Hood (1973). Why: 3 of 3 from the title's recent raters; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Fixes that worked when re-ranked: understand “not” in the request.
  [3] member 508, "a mystery to watch tonight, nothing too dark": Great Escape, The (1963) ranked above Holes (2003). Why: 2 of 3 from the title's recent raters, 1 of 3 from the member's own ratings; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Fixes that worked when re-ranked: none of the three.

Store recommendation: "understand “not” in the request" (worked for 9 of 10 most similar past failures). On held-out failures this kind of recommendation picked a working fix 37% of the time, vs 24% for always using "understand “not” in the request".

Write for a product manager, in plain everyday English: say 'ratings' (not links or edges), 'how sure the model is' (not confidence or probability), 'recent fans of the film' (not the title's recent raters); no jargon, no em dashes; short sentences.
Return JSON only, an object with keys:
  "diagnosis": one or two short sentences: what went wrong in this search and why;
  "precedent": one short sentence on what the similar past failures have in common with it, citing them;
  "recommendation": one short sentence on which fix to try and how far to trust it;
  "caveat": one short sentence on what this evidence does not show.

answer.diagnosis: The ranker put Aladdin (1992) first for "a fantasy movie that isn't animated" and seems to have missed the "isn't animated" part. It leaned on ratings from 2 of the 3 recent fans of Aladdin, and the model was 73% sure of its pick. When Aladdin's ratings were removed, how sure the model was fell to 46%, so those ratings drove the result.
answer.precedent: The closest past failures [1] and [2] were also requests with a "not" in them, where a title the member did not want ranked first, and [3] was a similar miss that the "not" fix did not repair.
answer.recommendation: Try the fix "understand 'not' in the request", which worked for 9 of 10 of the most similar past failures, but trust it only moderately because this kind of advice picked a working fix just 37% of the time, against 24% for always using that one fix.
answer.caveat: This evidence does not show that the ranker actually ignored the word "not", and one past case [3] was not fixed by it.
